opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core appeal is that they let us make use of a lot of data we already have, rather than requiring us to train new families of models from scratch.

Classic scaling laws, the compute-optimal kind, are fit by training a series of models within a single family where you carefully vary parameters, data, and compute. That's very informative, but it's expensive, and it mostly tells you about loss, which is a fairly abstract quantity. What we actually care about, for forecasting and governance, is something like "When will a model be able to do this specific task in the world? Autonomously write and debug a substantial piece of software, or assist meaningfully with some dangerous capability?" The link from loss to those downstream capabilities has historically been noisy and hard to pin down.

The observational approach says: there are now dozens or hundreds of publicly available models from different developers, trained with different recipes and different amounts of compute. If you look at how they perform across a broad set of benchmarks, it turns out that a lot of that variation can be captured by a small number of underlying capability dimensions. Something like a general capability factor, plus a few more specialized ones, such as coding or reasoning. Once you have that low-dimensional representation, you can relate it both to inputs like compute and to performance on more complex, agentic, or emergent tasks. That gives you a much richer and cheaper dataset for fitting trends.

A few things make this promising to me. First, it seems to predict some phenomena that looked like surprising jumps, so-called emergent capabilities, as fairly smooth functions of the underlying capability measures. That suggests some of the apparent unpredictability is an artifact of how we measure things, and that's very good news for anyone who wants early warning. Second, it lets you evaluate interventions, such as chain-of-thought prompting or other post-training techniques, and ask how their benefit scales, so you can anticipate how much elicitation might add on top of a raw model. Third, it's legible and reproducible. Outside researchers, governments, and evaluation bodies can do this kind of analysis without needing access to frontier training runs.

I'd add the obvious caveats. These are correlational fits across a heterogeneous population of models, so they can break when there's a genuinely new paradigm, such as a big shift in reinforcement learning on reasoning or in agent scaffolding. The benchmarks themselves can be saturated or contaminated. And real-world tasks are messier than any benchmark. So I see it not as an oracle but as one important instrument in a toolkit. For the broader project of making AI development go well, we need to get much better at seeing capabilities coming before they arrive, so that safety measures, evaluations, and policy can be in place in time. Anything that turns forecasting from guesswork into something more empirical and quantitative is, I think, really valuable.

r001.rationale: It says classic scaling laws mainly predict loss, while the link from loss to downstream capabilities has been noisy and hard to pin down.

r002.rationale: It describes analyzing varied existing models and relating capabilities to compute, but does not say the laws account for architectural differences in compute efficiency when extrapolating to future models.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic problem we face is that the capabilities we actually care about — can a model do a week of a software engineer's work, can it meaningfully assist with biology research, can it run a long autonomous project — are not the things that classic scaling laws predict. Classic scaling laws, the Kaplan and Chinchilla style results, tell you how loss on the next token goes down as you add compute and data. That's a beautifully smooth, predictable curve. But loss is a very abstract quantity. What we want to know is: when does the thing cross the threshold where it matters for the world? And the relationship between loss and downstream capability has historically looked jagged, with these apparent emergent jumps, which is exactly the kind of thing that makes forecasting hard and makes governance hard.

So the appeal of observational scaling laws — this is work out of Stanford, Yangjun Ruan and Chris Ré and Tatsu Hashimoto — is that instead of running your own expensive training runs across a compute sweep, you take the existing zoo of models that labs have already released, something like a hundred of them across different families, different sizes, different training recipes, and you treat them as the data. You look at how they all perform across many benchmarks, and it turns out that performance across these very different models is well explained by a small number of latent capability dimensions. Maybe three or so. Something like general reasoning, something like knowledge, something like coding. And those latent factors, in turn, move quite smoothly with compute, in a way that's roughly consistent across model families once you adjust for how efficient each family's training is.

Why does that matter for forecasting complex real-world tasks? A few reasons. One is sample efficiency: you get the statistical power of many training runs without paying for any of them, which means a small lab, an academic group, or a government evaluator can actually do this. Second, because you're working in this low-dimensional capability space, things that looked emergent and unpredictable in raw compute terms often look much more continuous once you plot them against the right latent factor. The jump wasn't a jump, it was a sigmoid you were looking at from the wrong angle. And third, and this is the part I find most important from a governance perspective, it gives you a principled way to extrapolate from the tasks we can measure today to the tasks we're worried about tomorrow. If a complex agentic task loads on the same latent capabilities that the benchmarks load on, you can ask: at what level of those capabilities does performance on this task start to take off? And then you can map that back to a compute scale, and from a compute scale to a rough timeline.

Now, I want to be honest about the caveats. The method is only as good as the benchmarks, and benchmarks saturate and get contaminated. The latent factors might shift as training paradigms change — post-training, reinforcement learning on reasoning, inference-time compute all complicate the picture, because they decouple capability from pretraining compute in ways that a simple compute-indexed law doesn't capture. And "complex real-world tasks" are often multiplicative: you need many sub-skills to all be good enough at once, and the aggregate can still have a sharp onset even if each component is smooth. So I don't think of this as a crystal ball. I think of it as moving us from "we were surprised by GPT-4" toward a regime where we can say, with error bars, "models with roughly this profile will probably be able to do roughly this by roughly then." For anyone trying to prepare institutions, safety evaluations, or policy in advance rather than scrambling afterward, that shift from surprise to anticipation is enormously valuable, even if the forecasts are imperfect.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts predictable next-token loss forecasts with downstream capabilities that matter in the real world, describing their relationship to loss as jagged and hard to forecast.

r002.rationale: It says observational scaling laws use existing models across families and adjust for each family’s training efficiency to relate latent capabilities to compute, supporting extrapolation to future tasks.

astra-6.text:
The basic attraction is that we’d like to forecast capabilities that we can’t yet directly observe. We want to know when models will be able to do consequential things in the world, and ideally we’d like some warning before they can actually do them.

Observational scaling laws offer a way to approach that by looking across existing models. You ask: how does performance on some task vary with a model’s broader capabilities? Perhaps the task is quite complicated, involving many steps, but performance nonetheless has a fairly predictable relationship with performance on a collection of simpler evaluations. If that relationship holds across models of different sizes and from different developers, that gives you some reason to think it captures something more general.

Then you can try to connect that relationship to our forecasts of how underlying model capabilities will improve. So you’re building a bridge from things we can measure and forecast relatively well to things we actually care about, like the ability to carry out a substantial research project.

Now, that’s a hypothesis to test, not a guarantee. Real-world performance depends on tools, how the system is organised, and whether it can reliably complete a long sequence of actions. Those can change the relationship. But the promising thing is that complexity doesn’t necessarily imply unpredictability. We may find fairly simple empirical regularities even for quite complex tasks, and those could make our forecasts substantially better.

r001.rationale: The response says complex capabilities are hard to observe and may be forecast through simpler evaluations, but it does not compare the maturity of those forecasts with forecasts for low-level benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It describes relationships across existing models of different sizes and developers, but does not say the laws account for architectural differences in compute efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that we can learn quite a lot from the differences between models that already exist. Rather than only asking how performance changes when you scale up one particular model family, you look across a range of models and ask whether their performance on some task follows a predictable relationship with their broader capabilities.

That’s potentially useful for complex real-world tasks, where we don’t have a clean theoretical account of what makes a model succeed. Imagine evaluating models on a research task. It might require knowledge, planning, writing code, and recovering from mistakes. You can measure how existing models do, and then ask whether there’s a relatively simple relationship between their general capability and their success on that task. If there is, you have some basis for forecasting what a more capable model might do.

Of course, the relationship could break down. A new training method or a better way of giving the model tools could change performance substantially. And you have to be careful about extrapolating beyond the range you’ve observed. But these relationships offer a way to make forecasts that are grounded in measurements, that we can test on subsequent models, and that can improve as we get more evidence. That seems much more promising than relying entirely on intuitions about which tasks look difficult.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forecasting complex real-world task performance, but does not compare this area with the more developed forecasting of low-level benchmarks.

r002.rationale: The response describes relationships between existing models’ general capabilities and task success, but does not say observational scaling laws account for architectural differences in compute efficiency.
